questions.q: How does this lab reuse the multi-cloud Terraform module pattern from Chapter 3?
options: It writes two separate, hand-maintained module sources, one per cloud
It calls the exact same module source twice, once for Azure and once for AWS, with only the inputs that genuinely differ supplied as variables
It avoids Terraform entirely and provisions both clusters manually in each cloud console
It uses a module that only supports Azure and adapts it for AWS afterward
questions.explain: The same module block is called twice -- once for the AKS cluster, once for the EKS cluster -- which is exactly the reuse pattern Lesson 11 established.

questions.q: What changes in the Deployment/Service manifest between the AKS deployment and the EKS deployment in this lab?
options: The replica count is doubled for AWS
The container image is rebuilt separately for each cloud
Nothing -- the same manifest file is applied unchanged to both clusters with kubectl
The API version has to be changed to a cloud-specific one
questions.explain: The Deployment/Service core is portable and nothing in it is cloud-specific, so the same file is applied with kubectl to both clusters unmodified.

questions.q: Why does the lab put storageClassName into separate per-cloud values files instead of hard-coding it into the shared manifest?
options: Because StorageClass names are never standardized across clouds, as Lesson 9 established, so this is exactly the kind of seam that has to be isolated rather than baked into the portable core
Because Kubernetes forbids StorageClass references inside a Deployment
Because values files are required for every Kubernetes object regardless of portability
Because AWS does not support PersistentVolumeClaims at all
questions.explain: managed-csi on AKS and gp3 on EKS are exactly the provider-specific names Lesson 9 warned don't travel, so they're isolated in small per-cloud files instead.

questions.q: What is the actual proof of portability demonstrated in this lab?
options: A design document claiming the workload is portable
One manifest file applied unmodified against two conformant clusters, producing the same running Deployment on both
A cost estimate showing AKS and EKS pricing is similar
A diagram showing both clouds connected by a VPN
questions.explain: Applying the same file with kubectl to both clusters and getting the same result is the concrete proof -- not a claim made on a slide.

questions.q: How does the lab verify that both deployments are actually behaving identically, rather than just assuming it?
options: By reading the Terraform plan output only
By checking that both clusters were created in the same calendar month
By comparing the containers' source code line by line
By running the same read-only kubectl commands -- checking replica count, ready status, and a healthz response -- against both clusters and comparing the output
questions.explain: Running identical get and exec/curl checks against both clusters and comparing results is what turns an assumption of identical behavior into a verified one.
